paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: What is street art? We have all seen it but maybe did not recognize it as art. Street art can be graffiti (scribbled names), or murals (large paintings on walls). It is surely therefore just art placed on the street, where the 'street' is taken in a very broad sense to mean, roughly, an urban space where anyone can go. However, this common sense answer cannot be right. In art markets around the world, paintings are often displayed in the street to attract potential customers, but this does not make them street art. Another answer is that street art is made somewhere else and subsequently placed in the street. This is true of some works, but as we will see, in many cases the street is employed in the production of the art. It does not help to add that the art must be in the street for at least a certain length of time. Street art includes works that range from the very short-lived – a matter of minutes, to much longer-lasting – a matter of years.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Josh Allen Harris creates inflatable creatures out of see-through plastic material and tapes them to subway air ducts on the sidewalks of New York City. When a subway train passes, air shoots out of the ducts and inflates the animals, casting them into a brief and frenzied existence. The inflatable sculptures last about as long as it takes for an average-sized chain of subway cars to zoom by. At the other extreme are the works of an artist known as 'Stikman'. One of Stikman's projects involves sticking little thermoplastic stickmen on the roadway in the middle of the street (normally in crosswalks). Unless they are deliberately destroyed, they will be there as long as the crosswalk is. The work of Invader, another street artist, is equally lasting. With powerful glue, he affixes mosaics (art that uses many tiny pieces of different colored materials to form a larger picture) depicting digital-style space creatures to various surfaces.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Other street artworks have a far less direct connection to the street, which raises the question of whether street art must be physically in the street. The artist Blu created Muto, a fascinating piece of animation that uses the street as a drawing board. Blu painted characters in his distinctive style on various street surfaces, took a photograph, shifted the character slightly by painting over his previous image, took another photograph, and so on. He then joined the images together to create a video with added sound effects. The result is a kind of real-life animation in which human-like figures appear to walk along walls, crawl under windows, and kick over logs; they lose their heads, expand, split in half, and multiply. One really must see it to believe it. Another example: Invader's mosaics are placed all over various cities, but the finished product is normally a map that details the whereabouts of each work. Invader prints the maps and distributes them in the 'invaded' city. The Paris and Los Angeles invasions are detailed in books and sold on Invader's website. These maps, and Muto, are arguably street art, even though they are not physically located in the street.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: It cannot be a necessary or sufficient condition that street art is art-in-the-street. Still, it obviously has some strong connection to the street. A different suggestion is that it is art that employs the street as an artistic resource. Now, there are different kinds of artistic resources. One kind of artistic resource is the physical material artists use to create their works. Just as painters use canvas, paint, frames, galleries, and walls, street artists use elements of the street. The subway and its brief shots of city air are literally part of Harris's sculptures: the street is the drawing board for Blu's animation: doorways, windows, sidewalks, signposts, rooftops -all are used to create street art. Another kind of artistic resource is the context in which the work is displayed. Some artists use the gallery, studio, or museum; street artists use the street. So perhaps an artwork is street art if, and only if, its creator uses the street as an artistic resource in at least one of these ways.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: This definition gets something right, but it is too inclusive. Posters and billboards use the street as an artistic resource – but they are not street art. So what is the distinction? The answer lies in the fact that street art's meaning is severely compromised when removed from the street. The artist C. Finley beautifies rugged steel dumpsters (large metal rubbish containers) by covering them with pretty wallpaper. That the wallpaper is on a dumpster is what makes it noteworthy. By covering dumpsters with such homey material, Finley draws attention to the fact that the street is also a kind of living room. Her work reveals that the elements of our shared public spaces need not be so uninviting. Wallpaper alone is merely pretty. Wallpaper on a dumpster: that is street art. Therefore, the material use of the street is internal to the meaning of street art. In contrast, the meaning of an advertisement does not change if it is removed from the street. Its message is generally buy this or see that no matter where it is. If removed, it might be ineffective, but it would still mean the same thing. If C. Finley's wallpaper is removed from the dumpster, or if the wallpapered dumpster is placed in a gallery, the meaning of the work will be severely compromised, if not entirely destroyed.
